## The question {auto-animate="true"}

::: r-fit-text
One of the most important things investors care is **given a portfolio and historical market behavior, how severe could future losses become?**
:::

- Traditional estimands, e.g. Beta, variance, does not directly present tail loss/the largest downfall in a period.
- I did a simple (right now) simulation study using bootstrap to get plausible future trajectories based on real historical data, then summarize downside risk.

![](riskpath_assets/crisis.png){width="80%"}



## Example portfolio for demonstration

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
| ETF  |  Weight | Exposure                     |
|:-----|--------:|:-----------------------------|
| VOO  | **50%** | S&P 500                      |
| QQQ  | **30%** | Nasdaq-100                   |
| SCHD | **20%** | Dividend-focused US equities |

**Initial investment:** \$10,000\
**2015-01-01 through 2026-01-01**
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
**Simulation settings**

- 150 trading days
- 5,000 simulated paths
- 10-day bootstrap blocks
:::
:::::



## From market prices to daily returns

1.  Download adjusted closing prices using `quantmod`.
2.  Align trading dates across VOO, QQQ and SCHD.
3.  Calculate daily simple returns for each ETF:

$$R_{t,j}=\frac{P_{t,j}}{P_{t-1,j}}-1$$

4.  Store the returns as a **days × 3 assets** matrix.

::: callout-note
returns <- na.omit(prices / lag(prices, 1) - 1)
returns <- as.matrix(returns)
:::



## Why a block bootstrap?

**Independent daily resampling** breaks the order of returns.

**Block bootstrap** instead samples short runs of consecutive historical days.

- Retains local patterns, including short-run volatility clustering.
- Samples the **same historical dates for all three ETFs**, preserving their within-day co-movement.
- Randomly joins blocks to create new return sequences.


## Bootstrap workflow: select, join, repeat

![](riskpath_assets/bootstrap.png){width="100%"}

**Illustration:** choose a random starting day → take 10 consecutive rows → sample another block → put them together → truncate to 150 days.



## Convert each resample into a portfolio path

For simulated day $t$:

$$r_{p,t}=0.50r_{VOO,t}+0.30r_{QQQ,t}+0.20r_{SCHD,t}$$

$$V_t=V_{t-1}(1+r_{p,t}),\qquad V_0=\$10{,}000$$

**Repeat 5,000 times** → matrix of **151 time points × 5,000 paths** (including day 0).

::: callout-note
technique used here: function, lapply, simulation
:::

## Measuring tail risk: VaR and ES

::::: columns
::: {.column width="57%"}
![](riskpath_assets/var.png){width="100%"}
:::

::: {.column width="43%"}
**Terminal loss:** $L=1-V_{150}/V_0$

**95% VaR: 11.98%**

95% of simulated terminal losses are at or below this threshold.

**Expected Shortfall: 17.94%**

Average loss among the worst 5% of outcomes.
:::
:::::


## Measuring the journey: maximum drawdown

::::: columns
::: {.column width="58%"}
![](riskpath_assets/drawdown.png){width="100%"}
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
$$D_s=\max_t\left(1-\frac{V_{t,s}}{\max_{u\le t}V_{u,s}}\right)$$

**Mean maximum drawdown:** 11.20%

**Probability of ≥20% drawdown:** 8.76%

A portfolio can recover by day 150 **and still experience a severe interim decline**.
:::
:::::


## Takeaways and limitations

**Takeaway:** Block bootstrap turns historical multivariate ETF returns into many potential portfolio trajectories, allowing both terminal-loss and path-dependent risk assessment.

**Important limitations**

- Future markets may behave differently from the historical sample.
- (Probably every model will) perform poorly when "Black Swan Event" happens, something like 2008 or COVID.
- Block length affects how much short-run dependence is retained. Also, there is the risk of wrong cutpoint.
- Results depend on portfolio weights, horizon and sample period.
